title: What fits in memory
objectives: Build a memory budget for training and for inference.

screens.title: A model's weights
screens.prose: A model with 7 billion parameters is stored in bf16, 2 bytes per parameter. A GB here is $10^9$ bytes.
screens.question: How many GB do the weights take?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the parameters by 2 bytes.

byKey.one: That is 1 byte per parameter, as in 8-bit. bf16 is 2.
byKey.fp32: That is float32, 4 bytes a parameter.

explain.text: 14 GB of weights: what inference must hold, before the KV cache.

screens.title: What training holds
screens.prose: Training holds more than the weights. Step through three settings and read the bytes each parameter needs.

state.caption: Inference in bf16: 2 bytes per parameter.

frames.caption: Inference in bf16: 2 bytes per parameter.
Training in float32 with Adam: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 bytes.

screens.question: How many bytes per parameter does training with Adam in mixed precision need?

options.why: That counts the bf16 weights, gradients and one float32 copy. Adam keeps two moments as well.
Each of Adam's two moments is 4 bytes; with the rest that is 16.
That is inference: the weights alone.

hints.text: Add the five bars of the mixed setting.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add up every bar of the mixed setting.

explain.text: Mixed precision does not shrink the training state: 16 bytes, the same as float32 with Adam. It saves time and activation memory, not optimiser memory.

canvas.caption: Mixed precision with Adam: 16 bytes per parameter.

screens.title: Training a 7B model
screens.prose: Train the 7-billion-parameter model with Adam in mixed precision: bf16 weights and gradients (2 + 2 bytes), Adam's two moments in float32 (4 + 4) and a float32 master copy (4).
screens.question: How many GB does the training state take, before activations?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply by all 16 bytes.

byKey.weights: That is the weights only, 2 bytes.
byKey.no-master: That leaves out the 4-byte master copy.

explain.text: 112 GB, eight times the weights, before a single activation is stored.

screens.title: A 70B model
screens.prose: Now 70 billion parameters, the same recipe.
screens.question: How many GB does training it take, before activations?

explain.text: 1,120 GB: no single chip holds it, so training a 70B model splits the state across many. Inference needs 140 GB.

screens.title: The tiny GPT
screens.prose: The tiny GPT has 18,017 parameters and trains in float64 with Adam: 8 bytes for each weight, gradient and moment, and no master copy.
screens.question: How many bytes is its training state?

byKey.one-moment: Adam keeps two moments, 16 bytes in float64.

explain.text: 576,544 bytes: a few hundred kilobytes. At this size the activations are the larger part, as the next screen shows.

screens.title: Activations for a batch
screens.prose: The tiny GPT's forward pass keeps every intermediate array for the backward pass: 705 float64 numbers per token. A batch is 16 windows of 32 tokens.
screens.question: How many bytes of activations does one batch keep?

hints.text: 512 tokens, 705 floats each, 8 bytes a float.

feedback.correct: $512 \times 705 \times 8 = 2{,}887{,}680$ bytes, five times the training state.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Tokens times floats per token times 8 bytes.

byKey.floats: That counts floats. Each float64 is 8 bytes.
byKey.window: That is one window of 32 tokens. The batch has 16.

explain.text: 2,887,680 bytes, 2.9 MB, of activations against 0.58 MB of weights and Adam state. Activations grow with batch and context, so they come on top of the 16-bytes rule and often dominate.

screens.title: Two bytes a parameter
screens.prose: A colleague plans to fine-tune the 7B model with Adam on one chip with 80 GB of memory: "it is 14 GB in bf16, so it fits five times over."
screens.question: What is wrong with the plan?

options.text: Training holds 16 bytes per parameter, 112 GB, which does not fit

options.why: That is the trap: 14 GB is the weights alone. Gradients, Adam's moments and the master copy make 112 GB.

options.text: Only the activations are missing; the rest fits
options.why: The state alone is 112 GB, above 80 before any activation.

options.text: It should be 28 GB, in float32
options.why: Even all in float32 the weights are 28 GB, and training needs 16 bytes each.

hints.text: What does training hold per parameter?
16 bytes with Adam in mixed precision.

feedback.correct: 112 GB of state before activations: the plan needs two chips or a lighter optimiser.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count what training holds.

byKey.ok: 14 GB is inference. Training needs eight times as much, 112 GB.

explain.text: Budgeting training at 2 bytes per parameter misses seven eighths of it. The state is 112 GB; activations come on top.

screens.title: Fits to serve, not to train
screens.prose: A 34-billion-parameter model and chips with 80 GB each. In bf16 it serves from one chip; training it with Adam in mixed precision does not fit there.
screens.question: At least how many 80 GB chips does the training state need, before activations?

hints.text: A chip cannot be split: round up.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide 544 by 80 and round up.

byKey.inf: One chip serves the model; training needs 544 GB.

explain.text: The same model fits one chip for inference and needs 7 to train, before activations. That is why many teams fine-tune with lighter optimisers or train only small added weights.

screens.title: Fewer bits for serving
screens.prose: **Quantisation** stores the weights in 8 or 4 bits for inference: memory halves or quarters against bf16. What it costs in accuracy must be measured on the task, not assumed.
screens.question: How many GB does the 70B model take at 4 bits?

explain.text: 35 GB at 4 bits. Real schemes also store a scale per small group of weights, a few per cent more, and the loss of accuracy differs by model and task: measure it.

screens.title: The memory budget
screens.prose:
For $N$ parameters:
$$\text{training} = N(b_w + b_g + b_{\text{opt}} + b_{\text{master}}) + \text{activations}$$
$$\text{inference} = N b + \text{KV cache}$$
With Adam in mixed precision the first bracket is 16 bytes.
screens.question: Which part of the training memory grows with the batch size?

options.why: They are per parameter, whatever the batch.
One gradient per parameter, summed over the batch.
The activations are kept per token, so they grow with the batch.

hints.text: Which terms are per parameter, and which per token?

feedback.correct: Activations are kept per token, so they scale with batch and context.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which term is counted per token?

explain.text: Every term but the activations is per parameter. A batch too large for memory is split into smaller micro-batches whose gradients are added.

screens.title: Sizing a research machine
screens.prose: A team will fine-tune a 7B model with Adam in mixed precision. At their batch and context the activations take 40 GB. The machines they can rent hold chips of 80 GB each.
screens.question: How many GB does the run need in all?

hints.text: Add the state and the activations.
Then compare with chips of 80 GB.

feedback.correct: $112 + 40 = 152$ GB: two 80 GB chips, with 8 GB to spare.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the two parts.

byKey.weights: That uses the 14 GB of weights instead of the 112 GB state.

explain.text: 152 GB fits on two 80 GB chips with little room; halving the batch frees activation memory if it does not fit. Budget memory before renting the machine.

ideas: Inference holds the weights (2 bytes each in bf16) and the KV cache: a 7B model is 14 GB, a 70B model 140 GB.
Training with Adam in mixed precision holds 16 bytes per parameter (weights 2, gradients 2, moments 8, master 4): 112 GB for 7B, 1,120 GB for 70B, before activations.
Activations grow with batch and context and can dominate; 8-bit and 4-bit weights halve and quarter inference memory, at an accuracy cost to be measured.
summary.trap: Budgeting training at the 2 bytes per parameter of inference: it is 16.

quiz.question: A 13B model is served in 8 bits with a 3 GB KV cache. How many GB does inference hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weights at 1 byte, plus the cache.

byKey.bf16: That is bf16 weights, 2 bytes each.
byKey.nokv: That leaves out the KV cache.

explain.text: 13 GB of 8-bit weights plus a 3 GB cache: 16 GB.
